literal: Ziji returned; at age six he inherited the title, which was reduced to duke.
idiomatic: When Ziji came home, his son at six inherited the rank, lowered to duke.

literal: Gaozu, because he succeeded the family estate while young, bestowed the name Zhi, style Chengye.
idiomatic: Gaozu, seeing him take up the house while still a boy, gave him the name Zhi, styled Chengye.

literal: Zhi was clever and talented, modest and fond of scholars.
idiomatic: Zhi was quick-witted and skilled, humble, and devoted to men of talent.

literal: As Forward General he followed Gaozu on the southern campaign and was appointed Minister of the Seven Arms, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, and Right General.
idiomatic: As forward general he followed Gaozu south and received the posts of minister of the seven arms, grand minister of ceremonies, and right general.

literal: In Shizong's time Hou Gang's son Yuan married Zhi's daughter.
idiomatic: Under Shizong, Hou Gang's son Yuan became Zhi's son-in-law.

literal: Gang was favored by Yuan Cha, and so Zhi was repeatedly promoted.
idiomatic: Gang stood high with Yuan Cha, and Zhi rose in rank again and again.

literal: He went out as Pacification Army Grand General, acting Inspector of Yangzhou, with acting title General Who Pacifies the South and command over all military affairs in Huainan.
idiomatic: He was sent out as pacification-army grand general and inspector of Yangzhou, with acting rank as general who pacifies the south and command of Huainan.

literal: Xiao Yan's generals Pei Sui and Yu Hong seized the outer wall of Shouchun; Zhi's sons were fierce fighters, and Sui found them hard to face, calling them the "little men of iron."
idiomatic: Pei Sui and Yu Hong of Liang seized Shouchun's outer ramparts; Zhi's sons fought like iron, and Sui, finding them hard to beat, called them the "iron boys."

literal: An edict ordered Prince of Hejian Chen to take overall command and reinforce him.
idiomatic: An edict put Prince of Hejian Chen in overall command to relieve him.

literal: Chen wished to give battle; Zhi, because the rains had lasted long, said they must still be cautious.
idiomatic: Chen wanted a pitched battle; Zhi, with the rains dragging on, urged restraint.

literal: Chen would not follow; they fought and the enemy took advantage; Zhi brought up the rear.
idiomatic: Chen refused; the enemy turned the fight, and Zhi covered the retreat.

literal: At first, because Zhi held strong forces yet would not decide battle for a long time, critics suspected ulterior designs.
idiomatic: At first, with strong troops under him and no battle for a long while, some suspected another design.

literal: The court again sent Prince of Hejian Chen, Prince of Linhuai Yu, and Minister of Writing Li Xian as three area commanders—outwardly to aid Zhi, inwardly in fact to guard against him.
idiomatic: The court sent Chen of Hejian, Yu of Linhuai, and Li Xian of the Masters of Writing as three commanders—nominally to help Zhi, in truth to watch him.

literal: When Xianyu Xiuli rebelled at Zhongshan, Zhi was made Grand Commander for the northern campaign.
idiomatic: When Xianyu Xiuli rose at Zhongshan, Zhi was made grand commander of the northern expedition.

literal: Shortly afterward, in his capacity as envoy he reached Ye.
idiomatic: Soon, still acting as envoy, he reached Ye.

literal: An edict relieved Zhi of the mobile secretariat and dismissed him as grand envoy; Prince of Hejian Chen was made Grand Commander and Li Daoyuan mobile secretariat.
idiomatic: An edict stripped Zhi of the mobile secretariat and envoy's powers; Chen of Hejian became grand commander and Li Daoyuan mobile secretariat.

literal: Zhi sent his son Ziyu with a memorial stating that he and Chen were together in Huainan, both facing the state's peril; Chen was defeated while he held the line, and private rancor arose.
idiomatic: Zhi sent his son Ziyu with a memorial: he and Chen had shared Huainan in national crisis; Chen lost while he held firm, and private bitterness followed.

literal: Moreover, seizing command on the spot was not his strength.
idiomatic: Besides, snatching command in the field was not his gift.

literal: The memorial was submitted but not accepted.
idiomatic: The throne did not accept it.

literal: Chen and Zhi went on ahead to Hutuo; Zhi did not yet wish to fight, but Chen would not follow.
idiomatic: Chen and Zhi reached Hutuo; Zhi still held back from battle, and Chen would not listen.

literal: On the march they reached Wulu; Xiuli intercepted them, and Chen did not go to the fight.
idiomatic: At Wulu, Xiuli ambushed them; Chen would not engage.

literal: When the rebels massed, they were utterly defeated; Zhi and Chen were both struck from the rolls.
idiomatic: The rebels gathered and routed them; Zhi and Chen were both removed from office.

literal: Soon afterward Shu rebelled in Zhengping commandery; Zhi was again given acting title General Who Pacifies the West and Commander to Suppress Shu, fought repeatedly with merit, was made General Who Pacifies the East, and restored to his former rank.
idiomatic: Shu soon rebelled in Zhengping; Zhi was again made acting general who pacifies the west and commander against Shu, won repeated victories, was made general who pacifies the east, and restored to his old title.

literal: Later he was made Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He later became right vice director of the Masters of Writing.

literal: Before long, Inspector of Yongzhou Xiao Baoyin held the province in rebellion; Zhi was again made mobile secretariat to suppress him.
idiomatic: Before long Xiao Baoyin rebelled as inspector of Yongzhou; Zhi was again sent as mobile secretariat to crush him.

literal: Zhi's back carbuncle had not yet healed; Empress Dowager Ling comforted him, saying: "Your ailment runs so deep; I wished to spare you, yet whom else can I rely on?
idiomatic: Zhi's back abscess was still unhealed; Empress Dowager Ling comforted him: "Your sore runs so deep; I would have spared you—yet whom else can I trust?"

literal: " Zhi answered: "After death one still serves; how dare I not exert myself?
idiomatic: Zhi answered, "One serves to the grave; how dare I hold back?"

literal: " At that time his son Ziyan also suffered crippling foot ailment and, leaning on a staff, came to take leave.
idiomatic: His son Ziyan, lame in both feet, came on a staff to bid farewell.

literal: Vice Director of the Masters of Writing Yuan Shun looked at his colleagues and said: "We fill the posts of great ministers, each in favor; on a day of peril, the sick go first—is that not wrong?
idiomatic: Vice director Yuan Shun glanced at his peers and said, "We hold great offices in favor; on a day of danger the sick march first—is that fitting?"

literal: " No one replied.
idiomatic: No one answered.

literal: At that time Xue Fengxian rebelled at Zhengping and Xue Xiuyi gathered forces at Hedong, seized the salt pools, besieged Puban, and east and west linked up in support of Baoyin.
idiomatic: Xue Fengxian rebelled at Zhengping; Xue Xiuyi massed at Hedong, held the salt pools, besieged Puban, and linked east and west to Baoyin.

literal: Zhi then held Hedong.
idiomatic: Zhi then secured Hedong.

literal: At that time there was an edict abolishing the salt-pool tax; Zhi submitted a memorial stating: "The salt pools are Heaven's gift of wealth, close to the capital region; they must be treasured and guarded and shared out with fair rule.
idiomatic: An edict abolished the salt-pool levy; Zhi memorialized: "The pools are Heaven's wealth at the capital's door; they must be guarded and rationed fairly.

literal: Now on four sides there are many alarms and the treasury is empty.
idiomatic: The borders are alarmed and the treasury bare.

literal: Yet the regular silk levies of Ji and Ding provinces are dying in disorder and can no longer be collected.
idiomatic: Ji and Ding are half lost; their regular silk dues cannot be gathered.

literal: Looking to the storehouses, outflow without inflow—there must be planning so expenditure and income balance.
idiomatic: The coffers spend without filling; income and outlay must be balanced.

literal: Roughly reckoning the salt tax for one year against silk, it should not fall short of three hundred thousand bolts—this is like setting Ji and Ding within the capital belt.
idiomatic: The salt tax alone, reckoned in silk for a year, should not fall short of three hundred thousand bolts—like moving Ji and Ding into the inner commanderies.

literal: If it is now abolished, the matter is like losing twice.
idiomatic: To abolish it now is to lose twice over.

literal: Your subject earlier disobeyed the stern order and did not first attack the border rebels but relieved Hedong—not because he was idle about Chang'an and urgent only for Puban.
idiomatic: I earlier defied your stern order and relieved Hedong before striking the border rebels—not because I slighted Chang'an for Puban.

literal: Once Puban fell, the salt pools would be lost and the army's mouth would be cut off—relief and supply would end.
idiomatic: Had Puban fallen, the pools would be gone, the army's ration cut, and supply ended.

literal: Heaven aided Great Wei; this plan did not miss.
idiomatic: Heaven aided Great Wei; the plan held.

literal: In Gaozu's years of rising peace there was no want, yet he still created salt officials and added custodians—not for goods and profit, but fearing that profit would corrupt custom.
idiomatic: Even in Gaozu's peaceful years, without want, he set salt officers and overseers—not for profit but lest profit corrupt custom.

literal: How much more now, when princes and dukes eat salary without work and officials hold posts without labor, rent taking six years' grain and levies folding next year's funds—these all come from private purses and seize men's strength.
idiomatic: How much more now, when nobles feast on salary and officials on empty posts, rent taking six years' grain and levies folding next year's funds—all from private purses, all seizing men's strength.

literal: It is not what I wish to say; the matter cannot be helped.
idiomatic: This is not what I wish to say; the matter cannot be helped.

literal: Your subject has already ordered the supervising office and commanders to lead their units and collect tax as usual, awaiting further edict."
idiomatic: I have ordered the supervising office and commanders to collect the tax as usual, pending further command."

literal: Zhi defeated Baoyin's general Hou Zhongde; Baoyin fled and Yongzhou was pacified.
idiomatic: Zhi routed Hou Zhongde, Baoyin's general; Baoyin fled and Yongzhou was pacified.

literal: He was made Inspector of Yongzhou.
idiomatic: He was made inspector of Yongzhou.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang's reign he was enfeoffed Prince of Shangdang, soon changed to Prince of Fengyi, then reduced to commandery duke.
idiomatic: At Zhuangdi's accession he was enfeoffed as prince of Shangdang, soon made prince of Fengyi, then reduced to commandery duke.

literal: He was transferred to Director of the Masters of Writing, added Palace Attendant, and concurrently Minister of Writing and Grand Mobile Secretariat, still garrisoning Chang'an.
idiomatic: He became director of the Masters of Writing, palace attendant, and concurrently minister of writing and grand mobile secretariat, still holding Chang'an.

literal: When the Deposed Emperor was enthroned he was transferred to Grand Marshal and Recorder of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne he was made grand marshal and recorder of the Masters of Writing.

literal: After the defeat at Hanling, Husi Chun first seized Heqiao and plotted to kill the Erzhu.
idiomatic: After Hanling, Husi Chun seized Heqiao first and plotted to kill the Erzhu.

literal: He sent Zhi into Luoyang to inform the emperor of the intent to execute Shilong and his brothers.
idiomatic: He sent Zhi into Luoyang to tell the emperor of the plan to kill Shilong and his brothers.

literal: At the beginning of the Emperor Who Fled the Capital he was transferred to Grand Tutor and Recorder of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: At the fleeing emperor's accession he was made grand tutor and recorder of the Masters of Writing.

literal: For merit in settling the succession he was further enfeoffed as Viscount Who Establishes the State.
idiomatic: For settling the succession he was further enfeoffed as viscount who establishes the state.

literal: Zhi memorialized asking to transfer the enfeoffment to his maternal cousin's son, Grand Minister of Justice Yuan Hongchao's second son Yun.
idiomatic: Zhi asked to pass the title to his cousin on his mother's side, Grand Minister of Justice Yuan Hongchao's second son Yun.

literal: At first Zhi's mother had died when he was born; Hongchao's mother raised him, and for that reason he sought to yield; it was granted.
idiomatic: His mother had died at his birth; Hongchao's mother raised him, and on that ground his request was granted.

literal: When the Emperor Who Fled the Capital entered the passes, Zhi was then garrisoning Hulao and followed to Chang'an.
idiomatic: When the fleeing emperor entered the passes, Zhi was at Hulao and followed him to Chang'an.

literal: Zhi's wife was the Zhang clan; she bore two sons, Ziyan and Ziyu.
idiomatic: Zhi's wife was Lady Zhang; she bore Ziyan and Ziyu.

literal: Later he had an affair with Lady Luo, killed her husband, abandoned Zhang and took Luo.
idiomatic: Later he took Lady Luo in secret, killed her husband, cast off Zhang, and married Luo.

literal: Luo was more than ten years older than Zhi and jealous and restrictive.
idiomatic: Luo was more than ten years his senior, jealous and controlling.

literal: Zhi in his grace loved and respected her; beside him there were no consorts or concubines; [10] among male and female attendants, those who died on suspicion of impropriety numbered several.
idiomatic: Zhi adored her and kept no other wives; [10] among servants, several died on mere suspicion.

literal: Luo bore three sons, Shaoyuan, Shiliang, and Jiliang; the brothers were all upright and martial.
idiomatic: Luo bore Shaoyuan, Shiliang, and Jiliang—brothers all upright and warlike.

literal: Zhi in youth was light and chivalrous, cockfighting and racing horses, striving and killing men; he fled for refuge to Longmen General Chen Xingde's house and was spared when an amnesty came.
idiomatic: Young Zhi was a swaggerer—cockfights, racing, brawls that killed; he fled to Longmen general Chen Xingde and was spared by amnesty.

literal: Thereupon he gave Luo's former husband's daughter, the Lu clan, in marriage, and married Xingde's elder brother Xingen to repay him.
idiomatic: He then married Luo's stepdaughter of the Lu clan to Xingde's brother Xingen in return.

literal: Ziyan, original name Jun, had great strength.
idiomatic: Ziyan, born Jun, was immensely strong.

literal: For repeated merit following his father on campaigns he was enfeoffed Viscount of Huaili.
idiomatic: For merit on his father's campaigns he was enfeoffed as viscount of Huaili.

literal: When the Emperor Who Fled the Capital and Duke Xianwu of Qi were at odds, Ziyan was added Central Army Grand Commander and Mobile Secretariat Vice Director, garrisoning Hongnong as a trusted pillar.
idiomatic: When the fleeing emperor and Duke Xianwu of Qi fell out, Ziyan was made central-army grand commander and mobile secretariat vice director at Hongnong as a trusted pillar.

literal: Later he followed the emperor into the passes.
idiomatic: Later he went with the emperor into the passes.

literal: Ziyan in youth once fell from a horse and broke his arm; bone stood up more than an inch above the elbow; he ordered the flesh cut open and the bone sawed, blood flowing several sheng, yet he spoke and jested as before.
idiomatic: As a youth Ziyan fell and broke his arm; bone jutted an inch above the elbow; he had the flesh opened and the bone sawed, lost pints of blood, and jested through it.

literal: Men of the time thought it surpassed Guan Yu.
idiomatic: Contemporaries said it surpassed Guan Yu.

literal: Ziyu held the post of Vice Director of the Chamberlain for the Palace.
idiomatic: Ziyu was vice director of the chamberlain for the palace.

literal: Collation notes
idiomatic: Textual notes

literal: In the tables of contents of all editions of Wei shu juan 25 this scroll is marked as lacunose.
idiomatic: Every edition's table of contents marks Wei shu juan 25 as lacunose.

literal: The Patchwork, Southern, and Jishui editions at the end of the scroll preserve Song-dynasty collation notes: "Wei Shou's book, Biographies section 13.
idiomatic: Patchwork, Southern, and Jishui editions keep Song notes at the scroll's end: "Wei Shou's book, Biographies 13.

literal: " The Bureau edition supplies below the character "lost."
idiomatic: " The Bureau edition adds "lost" below.

literal: The Palace Edition textual verification states: "Wei Shou's book is lacunose; later men supplemented it.
idiomatic: Palace Edition textual notes: "Wei Shou's text is missing; later hands supplied this.

literal: " On examination this scroll was supplemented from Beishi juan 22, the biographies of Changsun Song and Changsun Daosheng; the attached Changsun Zhi biography has overflowing wording that should come from the Gao clan Minor History.
idiomatic: " The received scroll was patched from Beishi juan 22 (Changsuns Song and Daosheng); the attached Zhi life has overflow wording likely from the Gao clan Minor History.

literal: Song led his old followers and township households, more than seven hundred families, in rebellion and flight. Beishi juan 22, Changsun Song biography, reads "township households" as "subordinate commanders."
idiomatic: "Song led his old followers and township households, more than seven hundred families, in revolt": Beishi juan 22, Song's life, has "township households" as "subordinate commanders."

literal: Commentary: "subordinate commanders" and "old followers" are set in contrast.
idiomatic: Note: "subordinate commanders" pairs with "old followers."

literal: "Old followers" means men of the Tuoba core; "subordinate commanders" should mean non-core tribal groups.
idiomatic: "Old followers" means core Tuoba men; "subordinate commanders" should mean non-core tribes.

literal: It is suspected that here "township households" was altered by later men.
idiomatic: "Township households" here was likely a later change.

literal: Thereupon Shusun Jian and others followed the river toward Luo and then entered the passes. Commentary: Those who followed the river toward Luo were the Wei army Shusun Jian led; those who entered the passes were the Jin army Liu Yu commanded—here the narrative is linked, so it seems Shusun Jian and others entered the passes.
idiomatic: "Shusun Jian and others followed the river toward Luo and entered the passes": the river march was Shusun Jian's Wei force; entering the passes was Liu Yu's Jin army—the linked narrative makes it seem Jian entered the passes.

literal: It is suspected the character for "Yu" has dropped above "then entered the passes."
idiomatic: Yu (Liu Yu) may have dropped before "entered the passes."

literal: Minister of Writing Liu Jie, Marquis of Wujing, Hou Anyuan, and others asked to pacify Feng Bo first. Juan 30, Anyuan biography, reads "Wujing" as "Wuyuan."
idiomatic: Minister Liu Jie, Marquis of Wujing, Hou Anyuan, and others asked to pacify Feng Bo first: juan 30, Anyuan's life, has "Wujing" as "Wuyuan."

literal: Commentary: Jin shu juan 15, Treatise on Geography, Lower, Xuzhou, Pengcheng commandery, has "Wuyuan county."
idiomatic: Note: Jin shu juan 15, Geography, Lower, Xuzhou, Pengcheng, lists Wuyuan county.

literal: The place did not belong to Wei, but at that time many enfeoffments took Southern-dynasty commandery and county names.
idiomatic: It lay outside Wei, yet many fiefs then took Southern-dynasty place-names.

literal: No county of "Wujing" is heard of; the character jing in this biography is suspected to be in error.
idiomatic: No "Wujing" county is known; jing here is likely wrong.

literal: The emperor then asked about hidden and manifest matters of the Celestial Master Kou Qianzhi. Beishi juan 22 reads "hidden" as "manifest omen"; "hidden" should be a corruption of "manifest omen."
idiomatic: The emperor asked the Celestial Master Kou Qianzhi about hidden and manifest matters: Beishi juan 22 has "hidden" as "manifest omen"; "hidden" corrupts "manifest omen."

literal: Du Chao approved it. Commentary: Du Chao has a biography in juan 83, Outer Kinsmen.
idiomatic: Du Chao approved. Note: Du Chao has a biography in juan 83, Outer Kinsmen.

literal: It may be the double name "Chaozhi," singly called "Chao," or the character zhi may have been added by contamination from "Kou Qianzhi" above.
idiomatic: This may be the double name Chaozhi, shortened to Chao, or zhi may have crept in from "Kou Qianzhi" above.

literal: In Emperor Gaozong's time he himself praised the weight of his forebears' merit. In various editions "zong" is written as "zu."
idiomatic: Under Gaozong he praised his forebears' merit: editions read zong as zu.

literal: Commentary: The matter appears in juan 5, Annals of Gaozong, at the end of the second year of Xing'an; "zu" is corrupt and is now corrected.
idiomatic: Note: the event is in juan 5, Gaozong Annals, end of Xing'an year 2; zu is wrong and is corrected.

literal: He was advanced in rank to Duke of Ruyin. Zhang Senkai states: "Earlier there was no text of an initial enfeoffment, yet it says 'advanced in rank'—suspected error.
idiomatic: He was advanced to duke of Ruyin. Zhang Senkai: "No prior enfeoffment is recorded, yet it says 'advanced'—likely error.

literal: " Commentary: This biography was supplemented from Beishi juan 22, Changsun Daosheng biography; it should be Li Yanshou's faulty abridgment.
idiomatic: " This life was patched from Beishi juan 22, Daosheng; the fault is Li Yanshou's abridgment.

literal: Such faulty abridgment appears again below—for example, "the emperor, because his grandfather Daosheng aided the founding court," without stating which emperor;
idiomatic: Such cuts recur below—"the emperor, because his grandfather Daosheng aided the founding court," without naming which emperor;

literal: "in his capacity as envoy reached Ye," without stating what envoy.
idiomatic: "as envoy reached Ye," without naming the mission.

literal: Not all collation notes are given here.
idiomatic: Further collation is not set out in full.

literal: His son Kang: Beishi juan 22 reads "Kang" as "Qiang."
idiomatic: His son Kang: Beishi juan 22 has Kang as Qiang.

literal: Beside him there were no consorts or concubines: Beishi juan 22 reads "consort-clan wives" as "concubines"; that reading is correct.
idiomatic: "Beside him there were no consorts or concubines": Beishi juan 22 has "consort-clan wives" as "concubines"; that is correct.
